How this book matches your board exam. Research check: this book follows NCERT Class 12 Introductory Macroeconomics, Chapters 1 and 2 (Introduction; National Income Accounting), for the CBSE 2026–27 session. The theory paper is 80 marks in 3 hours (Part A Macroeconomics 40 + Part B Indian Economic Development 40), with 20 marks for project work. Unit 1, National Income and Related Aggregates, carries 10 marks. Recent sample papers have 34 questions: in each part, 10 one-mark MCQs, two 3-mark, three 4-mark and two 6-mark questions. National income numericals (value added, income and expenditure methods) are regular 3–6 mark questions.

Each unit ends with a 10-mark practice set. All figures are invented for practice (in ₹ crore unless stated), and every calculation was checked by computer. The marking points are our own, not the official CBSE marking scheme.

Unit 1 of 10: Basic Concepts: Goods, Stocks and Flows, Investment

Key ideas

  • Final goods: goods for final use — consumption by households or investment by firms — not resold or used up in further production in the same year.
  • Intermediate goods: goods used up as raw material or for resale in the same year (e.g. flour bought by a baker).
  • The same good can be final or intermediate depending on its use (milk bought by a household vs by a sweet shop).
  • Consumption goods satisfy wants directly; capital goods are durable final goods used to produce other goods (machines, buildings).
  • Stock: measured at a point of time (wealth, capital, money supply). Flow: measured over a period (income, investment, depreciation).
  • Gross investment = addition to capital stock including replacement; net investment = gross investment − depreciation.
  • Depreciation (consumption of fixed capital): fall in the value of fixed capital due to normal wear and tear and expected obsolescence.

Worked examples

Example 1: Is a car bought by a taxi company a final or intermediate good? Answer: final (a capital good used for many years; not used up in the year).

Example 2: Gross investment ₹500 crore; depreciation ₹80 crore. Answer: net investment ₹420 crore.

10-mark practice set

  1. (1 mark, MCQ) Which is a stock? (a) income (b) wealth (c) investment (d) depreciation. Answer: (b).
  2. (1 mark) Why is a machine bought by a factory a final good? Answer: it is used for investment (production over many years), not used up in the same year.
  3. (3 marks) Classify as final or intermediate: (a) cloth bought by a tailor; (b) furniture bought by a school; (c) electricity used by a household. Answer: (a) intermediate (1); (b) final (capital good) (1); (c) final (consumption) (1).
  4. (2 marks) Distinguish between stock and flow with one example each. Answer: stock — at a point of time, e.g. capital (1); flow — over a period, e.g. investment (1).
  5. (3 marks) Net investment is ₹300 crore and depreciation is 20% of gross investment. Find gross investment. Answer: NI = 0.8 × GI (1); GI = 300 ÷ 0.8 (1); = ₹375 crore (1).

Common mistakes

  1. Classifying by the good instead of its use. 2. Calling income a stock. 3. Net investment = gross + depreciation. 4. Treating capital goods as intermediate. 5. Forgetting obsolescence in depreciation.

Quick recall

  1. Final good? 2. Stock example? 3. Flow example? 4. Net investment? 5. Another name for depreciation?

Answers: 1) For final consumption or investment. 2) Capital/wealth. 3) Income/investment. 4) Gross investment − depreciation. 5) Consumption of fixed capital.
